params.title: Principles
params.subtitle: Charge, voltage, current and power; magnetism; AC waves and meters; components, materials and semiconductors.

onScreen: Electricity from the ground up, then the exam facts built on it
scenes.narration: Welcome to Principles, the first lesson of Element 3. Everything a radio technician does rests on a few basic ideas about electricity: what voltage, current and resistance are, how power is measured, where magnetism comes from, and how alternating current behaves. We'll build those ideas from the ground up, assuming you've never studied electricity before. Then we'll use them to meet the parts found inside every radio: capacitors, coils, diodes and transistors, and the materials they're made from. By the end, you'll be able to answer every exam question in this subelement, and you'll know why each answer is right. Let's begin with the smallest piece of all.

params.title: Electricity is moving charge
items: Atoms hold tiny particles called electrons, each with a negative charge
Charge is measured in coulombs
Current: the flow of charge around a complete path, called a circuit
Current is measured in amperes: 1 ampere is 1 coulomb per second

onScreen: Current: flow of charge around a circuit
scenes.narration: Everything around you is made of atoms, and every atom holds even tinier particles called electrons. Each electron carries a small negative electric charge. Charge is what makes things push and pull on each other electrically: opposite charges attract, and like charges repel. We measure amounts of charge in coulombs. When charge moves along a path, such as a copper wire, that flow is called current. Current only flows around a complete loop, which we call a circuit. It's measured in amperes, or amps for short, and 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passing a point every second. Picture water in a pipe: current is like the amount of water flowing past a point each second.

params.title: Voltage: the push behind the current

callouts.label: Negative terminal: a crowd of extra electrons
Positive terminal: a shortage of electrons
Voltage, or EMF: the push between the terminals, in volts
No path, no current: connect a lamp and current flows

onScreen: Voltage, or EMF: the push, in volts
scenes.narration: What makes the charge move? A push, called voltage. A battery piles up extra electrons at its negative terminal and leaves a shortage at its positive terminal. Electrons want to even that out, and that urge is an electrical pressure, measured in volts. In the water picture, voltage is the water pressure that drives the flow. Voltage has another name you'll meet on the exam: EMF, electromotive force, which simply means the force that moves electrons. Notice that a battery sitting on a shelf has voltage across its terminals but no current, because there's no path. Connect a lamp between the terminals, and current flows.

params.title: Resistance: opposition to current, in ohms

onScreen: Resistance: opposition to current, in ohms
Resistance turns some energy into heat
Conductors: many loosely bound free electrons
scenes.narration: How much current flows for a given push depends on resistance: the opposition a material offers to current, measured in ohms. In the water picture, it's a narrow pipe holding the flow back. Forcing current through resistance turns some energy into heat, and parts built to have a chosen resistance are called resistors. Why do materials differ? It comes down to free electrons. In a metal such as copper, many electrons are only loosely bound to their atoms, so a voltage easily pushes them from atom to atom. That's why good conductors, with minimum resistance, have many free electrons. In an insulator such as glass, plastic or rubber, almost every electron is held tight, and almost no current flows.

params.title: Which metals conduct best?
items: Best low-resistance conductors: gold, silver and copper
Copper for wiring; silver and gold for plating and contacts
Higher resistance: stainless steel, bronze, lead and iron
Also higher: nickel, zinc and manganese

onScreen: Copper wiring; silver and gold plating
Higher resistance: stainless steel, bronze, lead, iron
scenes.narration: So which metals let their electrons move most freely, and have the lowest resistance? Gold, silver and copper are the best low-resistance conductors. That's why copper is used for wiring, and silver and gold for plating and switch contacts, where a clean, low-resistance connection matters most. Stainless steel, bronze, lead, iron, nickel, zinc and manganese all conduct too, but they have higher resistance. On the exam, the choices come as groups of 3 metals. Pick gold, silver and copper; every other group contains higher-resistance metals.

The exam also asks you to rank metals, using the word conductivity. Conductivity is the flip side of resistance: it says how easily a material conducts. You'll be asked for common materials in order of descending conductivity, meaning from best to worst. The order is silver, copper, aluminum, iron and lead. Silver is the best conductor of all, with copper a close second, which is why copper wire is everywhere. Aluminum comes next and is used where light weight matters. Iron and lead conduct far worse. Gold isn't in this list; it would sit between copper and aluminum. The trap answers scramble the order, so remember: silver, copper, aluminum, iron, lead.

params.title: Resistance and cross-sectional area
steps: Area: the size of the wire's cut end
params.answer: Halve the area, double the resistance

onScreen: Half the area: double the resistance
scenes.narration: The material isn't the only thing that sets a wire's resistance. Its size matters too. In this formula, R is the resistance, and resistivity is how strongly the material itself resists. Slice through a wire and look at the cut end: the size of that face is the cross-sectional area. A thick wire is like a wide pipe, with plenty of room for current. Resistance is inversely proportional to area: the 2 change by the same factor, in opposite directions. So halving the cross-sectional area of a conductor doubles its resistance, and doubling the area halves it. The trap answers say it halves, quarters or stays the same. And a longer wire adds resistance, just as a longer pipe adds drag.

params.title: Energy and power
items: Energy: the ability to do work, measured in joules
Power: how fast energy is delivered or used
The watt: the basic unit of electrical power
1 watt = 1 joule per second

onScreen: Power: how fast energy is used
scenes.narration: So far we've pushed current through wires and seen what holds it back. What's it all for? Flowing charge can do work: light a lamp, warm a heater, or send out a radio signal. The ability to do work is called energy, and energy is measured in joules. Power is how fast that energy is delivered or used. A heater and a night light might both run for an hour, but the heater uses far more energy, because it uses energy much faster: it has more power. The watt is the basic unit of electrical power, and 1 watt is 1 joule per second. So a 100 watt lamp uses 100 joules of energy every second it's on.

params.title: Power from volts and amperes
steps: A 6 volt battery drives 2 amperes through a lamp
More push or more flow: more power
params.answer: Unit of power: the watt, not the ohm, volt or ampere

onScreen: The watt, not the ohm, volt or ampere
scenes.narration: There's a handy way to find the watts. Power depends on how hard the charge is pushed, the voltage, and how much of it flows, the current. Multiply them: power in watts equals volts times amperes, so 1 volt pushing 1 ampere delivers 1 watt. In the water picture, that's pressure times flow. Let's try it. A 6 volt battery drives 2 amperes through a lamp. Volts times amperes is 6 times 2, so the lamp uses 12 watts: 12 joules every second. More push or more flow means more energy each second, so that makes sense. On the exam, the traps are the ohm, the volt and the ampere, which measure resistance, push and current.

onScreen: DC: one way only, from a battery
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
scenes.narration: Our battery pushes current one way only, steadily. That's DC, direct current. The power from a household outlet is different. Its voltage pushes one way, then reverses and pushes the other way, over and over. That's AC, alternating current. One full swing, out one way and back the other, is called a cycle. The number of cycles each second is the frequency, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle per second. Radio signals are AC too, just at far higher frequencies, thousands or millions of cycles every second. Most of this subelement is about AC, so let's look at its shape.

params.title: Where the sine wave comes from
labels: A dot on a wheel turning at a uniform speed
The dot's height at each instant traces the wave
Amplitude: the wave's height at any instant

onScreen: A dot on a wheel turning at uniform speed
Its height traces a sine wave
Amplitude: the height at any instant
scenes.narration: The smooth, natural shape of AC is called a sine wave. Here's where it comes from. Picture a wheel turning at a steady, uniform speed, with a dot painted on its rim. Watch only the dot's height: it rises to the top, sinks to the bottom, and comes back up. Plot that height against time, and you've drawn a sine wave. That's the exam's definition: a sine wave is a wave whose amplitude at any given instant can be represented by the projection of a point on a wheel rotating at a uniform speed. The projection is that height, like the dot's shadow cast sideways onto a wall, and amplitude just means the wave's height at that instant.

Because the sine wave comes from a turning wheel, we can measure progress along it in degrees, just like turns of the wheel. 1 full turn is 360 degrees, so there are 360 degrees in 1 complete sine wave cycle. The positive half, while the voltage pushes one way, spans 180 degrees, and the negative half spans the other 180. A quarter turn, from the start up to the top of the wave, is 90 degrees. On the exam, the traps for a complete cycle are 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Each of those is only part of the trip around. A complete cycle is always 360.

onScreen: Phase: where a wave is in its cycle, in degrees
In phase: peak together, 0 degrees apart
Out of phase: one peaks first; the gap is in degrees
scenes.narration: Degrees also let us compare 2 waves, using a word you'll need later: phase. Phase is where a wave is in its cycle at a given moment, measured in degrees. Picture 2 children on swings, pushed at the same rate. If they swing forward and back together, they're in phase. If one is at the top while the other is mid-swing, they're out of phase. AC waves of the same frequency work the same way. In phase, they rise and fall together, 0 degrees apart. Out of phase, one peaks before the other, and the gap is measured in degrees: a quarter cycle apart is 90 degrees. Coils and capacitors create exactly that gap, as we'll see.

params.title: The square wave
labels: Stays at each level for equal amounts of time
360° per cycle, like any repeating wave

scenes.narration: Not every AC wave is smooth. Digital circuits, the on-and-off circuits inside computers, often use a square wave, and so does test equipment. A square wave abruptly changes back and forth between 2 voltage levels, and it stays at these levels for equal amounts of time: half of each cycle high, half low. On a screen it looks like the top of a castle wall. Like any repeating wave, it has 360 degrees in a cycle, so the trap answer of 300 degrees is wrong. And it isn't always positive or always negative: it can swing above and below zero.

params.title: Building a square wave from sine waves

blocks.label: Fundamental
blocks.note: A sine wave at the wave's own frequency

blocks.label: Square wave
blocks.note: Edges sharpen as harmonics are added

onScreen: Add the 5th, 7th and all odd harmonics
scenes.narration: How can sharp corners come from smooth sine waves? Here's a surprising fact: any repeating wave, however sharp its corners, can be built by adding sine waves together. The lowest one, at the wave's own frequency, is called the fundamental. The others are harmonics: sine waves at whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency. The 2nd harmonic is twice the frequency, the 3rd is 3 times, and so on. The odd harmonics are the 3rd, 5th, 7th and onward. A square wave is made up of sine waves of the fundamental frequency and all the odd harmonics. Each odd harmonic you add sharpens the edges, and the more you add, the squarer the wave becomes.

params.title: The sawtooth wave
labels: A slow, steady ramp, then a fast snap back
Rise and fall times very unequal
Made of the fundamental plus all harmonics, even and odd

onScreen: Rise and fall times very unequal
scenes.narration: Now a third shape, the sawtooth wave. It ramps steadily in one direction, then snaps back, like the teeth of a saw. Rise time is how long a wave takes to climb, and fall time is how long it takes to drop back. On a sawtooth, the 2 are very different; that's its signature. A sawtooth wave is characterized by a rise time significantly faster than its fall time, or the other way around. In this picture, the slow part is the rise and the fast part is the fall. Test instruments use the ramp to sweep a dot across their screens. It's made of sine waves at the fundamental frequency and all the harmonics, even and odd.

params.title: Square wave versus sawtooth wave
rows: A slow ramp and a fast edge
One much faster than the other

onScreen: Square: 2 levels, sawtooth: ramp and edge
Square rises and falls equally fast
Square: odd harmonics; sawtooth: all harmonics
scenes.narration: Let's put the 2 side by side, because the exam likes to swap them. The square wave sits at 2 levels for equal times, while the sawtooth has a slow ramp and a fast edge. The square wave rises and falls equally fast; the sawtooth doesn't. And the square wave is built from the fundamental plus only the odd harmonics, while the sawtooth uses all the harmonics, even and odd. Sine, cosine and tangent waves are the usual wrong answers. A cosine wave is just a sine wave shifted by a quarter cycle, so like a pure sine wave, it's a single frequency with no harmonics at all. The takeaway: odd harmonics only, square; all harmonics, sawtooth.

params.title: How big is an AC wave?
labels: Peak: from the center line to the top
Peak-to-peak: from the top to the bottom

scenes.narration: We can name a wave's shape. Now, how do we say how big it is? An AC voltage is always changing, so there are several ways to give its size, and the exam uses all of them. The center line is where the voltage is 0. Measure from that center line up to the top of the wave, and you have the peak voltage. Measure from the very top all the way down to the very bottom, and you have the peak-to-peak voltage. A sine wave's 2 halves are mirror images, so its peak-to-peak value is always twice its peak. Keep this wave in mind; we'll mark more levels on it as we go.

params.title: Reading a wave on an oscilloscope

callouts.label: Graticule: the grid of squares over the screen
Vertical control: how many volts each square stands for
Peak-to-peak: count squares from the top of the trace to the bottom

scenes.narration: To actually see those levels, you use an oscilloscope: an instrument that draws voltage up its screen against time across it. Over the screen lies the graticule, a grid of squares for measuring. The vertical control sets how many volts each square stands for. So which voltage is easiest to measure on a pure sine wave? Peak-to-peak. You just count the squares from the top of the trace, the line the wave draws, to the bottom, without even finding the center line. The other ways of stating a wave's size, which we're about to meet, have to be calculated from that reading, and a DC value doesn't describe a sine wave at all.

blocks.label: AC voltage of equal RMS value
Exactly the same heat
blocks.note: That's why RMS is the effective value

onScreen: AC of the same RMS value: the same heat
scenes.narration: Here's a puzzle. An AC voltage keeps changing, so which single number tells you how strong it is? The answer is about heating. Connect a steady DC voltage to a resistor, and it warms up. Now find the AC voltage that warms the same resistor exactly as much. That value is the RMS voltage. RMS, root mean square, is the AC voltage that causes the same heating in a resistor as a corresponding value of DC voltage, which is why it's also called the effective value. The name describes the math: square the voltage at every instant, take the mean, or average, then take the square root. For a sine wave, RMS works out to 0.707 times the peak.

callouts.label: Selector on AC volts or AC amps
RMS: root mean square. There is no such measure as TRM
Household outlet: about 117 V AC RMS

scenes.narration: Because the effective value is what matters for heating and power, AC meters are built to show it. A voltmeter measures voltage, an ammeter measures current, and a multimeter does both. Set the selector to AC volts or AC amps, and the reading is an RMS value: an AC ammeter indicates effective, or RMS, values of current, and an AC voltmeter shows RMS voltage. Watch for a trap answer that says T R M. There's no such measure; the letters are R M S, root mean square. Put the meter on a common household outlet, and it reads about 117 volts AC, the outlet's RMS voltage. You'll hear 115 or 120 volts quoted too, but the exam's answer is 117 volts.

params.title: From the meter reading to peak voltage

scenes.narration: Your meter shows RMS, but sometimes you need the peak, for example to know whether a part can survive the highest voltage in each cycle. The rule: multiply the voltage shown on an AC voltmeter by 1.414 to get the peak. Where does 1.414 come from? It's the square root of 2, which is 1 divided by the 0.707 we just met. Let's try it on the outlet. The meter says 117 volts, and 117 times the square root of 2 is about 165.5 volts, so that's the peak. Double it for peak-to-peak: about 331 volts. To go the other way, from peak back to RMS, multiply by 0.707. That's the trap answer when a question asks for the peak.

params.title: The household outlet: 3 levels on 1 wave
labels: RMS: 117 V, what the meter reads
Peak: 165.5 V, center line to top

scenes.narration: Let's mark those outlet numbers on our sine wave, because the exam tests all 3 levels. The meter reading, the RMS value, is 117 volts. The peak, from the center line to the top, is 165.5 volts. And from the top all the way to the bottom, the peak-to-peak value is 331 volts. When the exam asks for the peak, it offers 331 volts as a trap: that's peak-to-peak, twice the peak. Another trap, 234 volts, is just 117 doubled, which matches none of these levels. And 82.7 volts comes from multiplying 117 by 0.707, the wrong direction. Peak at the outlet: 165.5 volts.

params.title: From the meter reading to average voltage
steps: Average over a half cycle = 0.637 × peak

scenes.narration: One more conversion. The average voltage is the wave's average height over half a cycle. Why only half? Over a whole cycle, the positive and negative halves cancel out to 0. For a sine wave, the half-cycle average is 0.637 times the peak, while RMS is 0.707 times the peak. Divide one by the other, and the average comes out at about 0.9 times the RMS value. So to get the average voltage, multiply the voltage shown on an AC voltmeter by 0.9. Lock in the 2 factors: times 1.414 for peak, times 0.9 for average. The 3.14 in the answer choices is pi, which belongs to neither.

params.title: The capacitor: energy in an electric field
items: 2 metal plates separated by an insulator, called the dielectric
Charge it: electrons pile up on one plate and leave the other
The energy is stored in the electrostatic field between the plates
Capacitance, in farads: how much charge it holds per volt

onScreen: 2 plates and an insulator, the dielectric
Charge piles up on one plate
Energy in the electrostatic field between the plates
scenes.narration: That's how AC is measured. Now let's meet the parts inside every radio, starting with the capacitor. A capacitor is 2 metal plates separated by an insulator, called the dielectric. Connect it to a battery, and electrons pile up on one plate while the same number leave the other. No current crosses the insulator, so the charge stays put. It took work to crowd those electrons together, and that work is stored in the electrostatic field, also called an electric field, that the separated charges create between the plates. So the device that stores electrical energy in an electrostatic field is the capacitor. How much charge it holds for each volt is its capacitance, measured in farads.

params.title: Joules, coulombs or watts?
rows: Energy stored in a capacitor's field
How fast a lamp uses energy

onScreen: Joules: energy, such as the energy in a capacitor's field
scenes.narration: So a capacitor holds energy. How is that energy measured? The exam asks what term expresses the amount of electrical energy stored in an electrostatic field. The answer is joules, because joules measure energy of every kind, including the energy waiting in a capacitor's field. 2 wrong answers sound close. Coulombs measure charge, the amount piled onto a plate, not the energy stored. Watts measure power, the rate at which energy flows, not an amount. Volts are wrong too: they measure the push. So energy in a field is counted in joules.

params.title: Capacitors in parallel
steps: Parallel: side by side, across the same 2 points
Like one capacitor with bigger plates
Series capacitors: use the sum of reciprocals

onScreen: C sub T = C sub 1 + C sub 2 + C sub 3
scenes.narration: Circuits often combine capacitors, so we need 2 words. Parts in parallel sit side by side, each connected across the same 2 points. Parts in series are connected end to end, in a single path. 3 capacitors in parallel act like a single capacitor with bigger plates. Bigger plates hold more charge, so the capacitances simply add: C sub T, the total, equals C sub 1 plus C sub 2 plus C sub 3. Capacitors in series are the opposite case. Chaining them is like widening the gap between the plates, so the total shrinks. It's found with the sum-of-reciprocals formula, a reciprocal being 1 divided by a number, and that formula is the trap for parallel.

blocks.label: Magnetic field
blocks.note: Circles of force around the wire

onScreen: Current through a conductor makes a magnetic field
Circles of force around the wire
Voltage with no current: no magnetic field
scenes.narration: A capacitor keeps its energy in an electric field. There's a second kind of field in electronics, the magnetic field, and it comes from current. Whenever current flows through a conductor, it produces a magnetic field around it: invisible circles of force wrapped around the wire. Hold a compass near the wire, and the needle swings. The key is movement. Moving charge makes magnetism; charge sitting still does not. Remember the battery on the shelf, with voltage across its terminals but no current? A DC source that isn't connected to a circuit makes no magnetic field. Neither does a charged capacitor, whose charge just sits on its plates. In short: current makes magnetism; voltage alone doesn't.

params.title: What sets the field's strength?
items: The amount of current sets the strength of the field
Double the current, and the field doubles
Resistance and wire diameter matter only by changing the current

onScreen: Field strength: set by the amount of current
Double the current, double the field
Resistance and diameter only change the current
scenes.narration: So what determines how strong that magnetic field is? The amount of current. The field is directly proportional to the current, which means the 2 rise and fall in step: double the current, and the field doubles; halve it, and the field halves. That makes sense: every moving electron adds its share of magnetism, so twice the flow gives twice the field. The exam's other choices mention resistance, ratios of current and resistance, or the diameter of the wire. Those matter only because they change how much current flows. The field itself answers to the current alone.

params.title: Coils and magnetic flux
items: Wind the wire into a coil: the fields of the turns add up
Lines of force: how we draw a magnetic field
Flux: the lines of force, taken together
Magnetic circuit: the closed path the lines of force follow

onScreen: A coil adds up the fields of its turns
Lines of force: a drawing of the field
Flux: the lines of force together
scenes.narration: More current is one way to get a stronger field. Shape is another. 1 straight wire makes only a weak field, but wind the wire into a coil, and the fields of all the turns add together, making a strong field through the middle, just like a bar magnet. We draw a magnetic field as lines of force, showing which way it points and how strong it is. The lines of force, taken together, are called magnetic flux. These lines never just stop: they always form closed loops, running through the coil and back around the outside. The closed path they follow is called a magnetic circuit, much as current follows an electric circuit.

onScreen: Electric circuit: current; magnetic circuit: flux
Reluctance: opposition to creating lines of force
scenes.narration: A magnetic circuit even has its own version of resistance. In an electric circuit, current flows and resistance opposes it. In a magnetic circuit, flux is set up, and reluctance opposes it. Reluctance is the opposition to the creation of magnetic lines of force in a magnetic circuit, the magnetic counterpart of resistance. Air has high reluctance. Iron has low reluctance, so flux builds easily in it, which is why coils are often wound around a core, a piece of iron or similar material through the middle. On the exam, the wrong answers are eddy currents, hysteresis and permeability. Eddy currents and hysteresis are ways an iron core wastes energy as heat, and permeability, coming next, is the opposite idea.

params.title: Permeability and reluctance
rows: Opposition to creating lines of force

scenes.narration: So what is permeability? It's how readily a material lets lines of force pass through it. Formally, permeability is the ratio of the magnetic flux density in a substance to the magnetizing force that produces it. Flux density is how tightly packed the lines of force are. Magnetizing force is the push that the coil's current provides. Give the same push to an iron core and to air, and the iron packs in far more lines of force: its permeability is high. Iron and ferrite, a ceramic made with iron oxide, have high permeability. On the exam, look for the word ratio: flux density divided by magnetizing force. So iron has high permeability and low reluctance; the 2 go together.

onScreen: whose field opposes the change: Lenz's law
scenes.narration: We've seen that current makes a magnetic field. It also works the other way. When a magnetic field around a conductor changes, growing or shrinking, it induces, or creates, a voltage in that conductor. That's called induction. It's how generators make electricity, and how a transformer, 2 coils sharing one magnetic field, passes energy from one coil to the other. If there's a complete path, the induced voltage drives an induced current, and that current makes a magnetic field of its own. Which way does that new field point? Always against the change that caused it. When induced currents produce expanding magnetic fields that oppose the original magnetic field, that's Lenz's law. Gilbert's, Maxwell's and Norton's laws are the exam's decoys.

params.title: Back EMF: the coil pushes back
items: A coil's own changing field induces a voltage in the coil itself
Lenz's law sets its direction: against the change
Back EMF: a voltage that opposes the applied EMF
It is a voltage, not a current

onScreen: A coil's own changing field induces a voltage
Back EMF opposes the applied EMF
scenes.narration: Lenz's law has a striking result in a single coil. Change the current through a coil, and its own changing magnetic field sweeps across its own turns, inducing a voltage in the coil itself. By Lenz's law, that voltage pushes against the change. Remember that EMF, electromotive force, is another name for voltage. The applied EMF is the voltage you put across the coil, and the induced voltage that fights it is called back EMF, or counter EMF. So back EMF is a voltage that opposes the applied EMF. It's a voltage, not a current, which rules out 2 of the exam's choices, and the choice about R times C percent is made up.

params.title: The inductor: energy in a magnetic field
rows: Stores it in the electrostatic field
Stores it in its magnetic field
Passes it from one coil to another

scenes.narration: Put the last few ideas together and you have a new part: the inductor, which is simply a coil of wire used as a circuit component. Compare it with the capacitor. The capacitor stores energy in the electrostatic field between its plates. The inductor stores energy in its magnetic field instead: while current flows, the field holds energy, and when the current falls, the collapsing field hands it back. Because of back EMF, an inductor resists any change in its current. Its inductance, measured in henrys, says how strongly. On the exam, the other storage choices are the battery, which stores energy chemically, and the transformer, which passes energy from one coil to another rather than storing it.

params.title: Changing an antenna coil's inductance
rows: Iron or ferrite packs in flux
Turns link each other more tightly

scenes.narration: How much inductance a coil has depends on how it's built. Antenna systems often use a coil to tune the antenna, adjusting it to suit the frequency in use, so you may need to change the coil's inductance. Turns matter most: inductance grows with the square of the number of turns, so doubling the turns gives about 4 times the inductance. To reduce the inductance of an antenna coil, reduce the number of turns. Every other choice the exam offers raises it instead. Adding turns raises it. Adding core permeability, with an iron or ferrite core, packs more flux into the coil. Compressing the turns lets more of each turn's field pass through its neighbors, which raises it too.

params.title: Inductors in series
steps: Series: end to end, in one path
Adds just like resistors in series

onScreen: L sub T = L sub 1 + L sub 2
scenes.narration: Now combine inductors. Connect 2 in series, end to end, and the same current passes through both coils, so their effects add up. The total inductance is L sub T equals L sub 1 plus L sub 2. That adds just like resistors in series, which add because the current must fight through each one in turn. For example, a 2 henry coil in series with a 3 henry coil gives 5 henrys. Inductors in parallel use the reciprocal formula instead, so that's the trap for series. Notice the mirror image: inductors add in series, while capacitors add in parallel.

params.title: Inductive reactance of a coil
steps: Higher f or bigger L: more opposition

onScreen: X sub L: reactance in ohms
scenes.narration: Until now, our coils have carried steady current. What happens when you feed AC to a coil? The current keeps changing, so back EMF keeps fighting it, and the coil opposes the AC. That opposition is called inductive reactance, and like resistance, it's measured in ohms. Its symbol is X sub L. From the frequency and the inductance, X sub L equals two pi f L. Pi is the familiar 3.14 from circles, f is the frequency in hertz, and L is the inductance in henrys. The faster the current changes and the bigger the coil, the harder it pushes back: double the frequency, and the reactance doubles. The exam's look-alike, pi f L, drops the 2.

onScreen: DC: a coil passes it, a capacitor blocks it
Higher frequency: coil opposes more, capacitor less
Coil: X sub L = 2π f L
Capacitor: X sub C = 1 / 2π f C
scenes.narration: A capacitor reacts to AC too, but in the opposite way. Start with DC. A coil is just wire, so steady DC passes straight through it. A capacitor has an insulator between its plates, so it blocks DC. AC is different: it charges the plates one way, then the other, so current keeps flowing back and forth in the wires. The higher the frequency, the less time the plates have to fill up and push back before the voltage reverses. So as frequency rises, a capacitor opposes AC less, while a coil opposes it more. That's capacitive reactance, X sub C, equal to 1 over two pi f C, with C in farads, and it's the trap answer for a coil.

blocks.label: Supply line
blocks.note: DC with unwanted AC riding on it

blocks.label: Bypass capacitor
blocks.note: Low impedance path for AC; blocks DC

onScreen: Supply line: DC with unwanted AC
Bypass capacitor: low impedance path for AC
scenes.narration: Now let's put a capacitor to work. First, one more word: impedance, the total opposition a circuit offers to AC, resistance and reactance together, also measured in ohms. Suppose a supply line carries DC to a circuit, with some unwanted AC, such as noise, riding on it. Connect a capacitor from the line to ground, the circuit's common return point. To AC, that capacitor is a low impedance path, an easy shortcut, so the AC escapes to ground. To DC, the capacitor is a wall, so DC carries on to the circuit. That's a bypass capacitor: it removes alternating current by providing a low impedance path to ground. The trap says it shunts, or diverts, DC to ground: exactly backward.

Coils and capacitors also shift the timing of AC, which changes how we count power. Here's where phase comes back. In a resistor, current rises and falls with the voltage: they're in phase, and all the energy turns into heat. In a coil, back EMF delays the current, so it peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage: 90 degrees out of phase. In a capacitor, current peaks a quarter cycle early: it flows hardest while the plates are empty and just starting to fill, before the voltage builds up. Either way, for part of each cycle the current flows against the voltage, sending energy back to the source. So with coils and capacitors, volts times amps isn't the whole story.

params.title: Apparent power
steps: Ignores phase, so it can overstate the work

onScreen: Apparent power = voltmeter reading × ammeter reading
scenes.narration: So let's be careful with meter readings. Multiply the reading of an AC voltmeter by the reading of an AC ammeter, and the product is called apparent power. It's measured in volt-amperes, not watts. It's called apparent because it's what the power appears to be from the meters alone. But the meters show RMS values and say nothing about phase. If the voltage and current are out of phase, some of that apparent power is only borrowed and returned, so the real work done is less. Finding the true power takes a second number, the power factor, coming up next. On the exam, the product of the 2 readings is apparent power, not true power, power factor or current power.

params.title: True power: the power actually used
params.formula: True power = apparent power × power factor
steps: Power factor: the fraction doing real work, 0 to 1
True power is in watts: the power dissipated
params.answer: Multiply apparent power by the power factor

onScreen: True power = apparent power × power factor
scenes.narration: How do you find the power that's really used, the power dissipated as heat, light or radio waves? That's the job of the power factor: the fraction of the apparent power that does real work, somewhere between 0 and 1. For a pure resistance, voltage and current are in phase, and the power factor is 1. The more out of phase they are, the smaller it gets. True power equals apparent power times the power factor, and it's measured in watts. The traps: RMS voltage times RMS current alone gives only the apparent power, and dividing by the power factor or subtracting it are made up.

params.title: Reactive power: borrowed and returned
items: The out-of-phase power of inductors and capacitors
Measured in VAR: volt-amperes reactive
Stored in a field, then returned each cycle
Does no net work

onScreen: Reactive power: out-of-phase power of coils and capacitors
scenes.narration: What about the part that isn't true power? The out-of-phase power associated with inductors and capacitors is called reactive power. It's measured in VAR, volt-amperes reactive. Think of it as energy borrowed and paid back. During one part of each cycle, a coil stores energy in its magnetic field, or a capacitor stores it in its electric field. During the next part, that energy is handed back to the source. Because it's returned every cycle, reactive power does no net work. The exam's decoys are effective power, true power and peak envelope power, which is a transmitter rating. Only reactive power is the out-of-phase kind.

params.title: Coil and capacitor: energy swaps back and forth

blocks.label: Coil's magnetic field
blocks.note: Holds the energy for part of a cycle

blocks.label: Capacitor's electric field
blocks.note: Holds it for the next part

scenes.narration: Put a coil and a capacitor in the same circuit, and something neat happens. Their timing is opposite, because a coil's current lags the voltage while a capacitor's leads it. When the coil gives energy back, the capacitor takes it in, and then the reverse. So the reactive power alternates between the coil's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field, back and forth, cycle after cycle. It is not dissipated. Only resistance turns electrical energy into heat. The exam's wrong answers all say the reactive power is dissipated: as heat, as fields, or as kinetic energy. It isn't dissipated at all; it just swaps between the 2 fields.

params.title: Apparent, true and reactive power
rows: Stored and returned; no net work

scenes.narration: Let's line up the 3 kinds of power, because the exam mixes up their names. Apparent power is what the meters suggest: voltmeter reading times ammeter reading, in volt-amperes. True power is what actually gets used: apparent power times the power factor, in watts, the same watt that's 1 joule per second. Reactive power is the out-of-phase part, in volt-amperes reactive. It's stored and returned each cycle and does no net work. When voltage and current are in phase, as in a plain resistor, apparent power equals true power, and there's no reactive power at all.

onScreen: Load impedance equals the source's internal impedance
scenes.narration: One last idea about power: getting the most out of a source. Every real source, even a battery, has some resistance inside it: its internal resistance. What it powers, such as a lamp or an antenna, is the load. Make the load's impedance very low, and most power is wasted in the source. Make it very high, and hardly any current flows. The best is in between: with the internal resistance fixed, maximum power is transferred to the load when the load impedance equals the internal impedance of the source. At that match, half the power is lost in the source, but the load gets more than at any other value. The traps say the load should be greater or less than the source.

blocks.label: Frequency increases
blocks.note: RF current crowds into a thin surface layer

blocks.label: AC resistance rises
blocks.note: Less of the conductor carries current

onScreen: Low frequency: current uses the whole wire
Higher frequency: RF current near the surface
scenes.narration: So far we've treated wires and insulators as perfect. Real materials have quirks, especially at radio frequencies and at sea. Start with the copper itself. At DC and low frequencies, current spreads through the whole thickness of a wire. RF, radio frequency, current behaves differently. As the frequency increases, the wire's own rapidly changing magnetic field pushes the current outward, so it flows in a thin layer closer to the surface. That's called skin effect. With only a thin skin carrying current, it's as if the wire got thinner, and you know what that does: its AC resistance rises. That's why RF conductors are often silver plated or hollow. The traps say it happens as frequency decreases, or blame heat.

params.title: Relative dielectric constant
items: Dielectric constant: a material's capacitance compared with a vacuum
A vacuum is defined as exactly 1
Air, at about 1.0006, is taken as 1
Glass, mica and plastics are higher

onScreen: Dielectric constant: compared with a vacuum
scenes.narration: Insulators matter as much as conductors, especially inside capacitors. Remember the dielectric, the insulator between a capacitor's plates. The relative dielectric constant tells you how much more capacitance a material gives you than empty space would. A vacuum, completely empty space, is the reference, and it's defined as exactly 1. Air is so close to a vacuum, about 1.0006, that its relative dielectric constant is taken as 1. Solid insulators such as glass, mica and plastics have higher values, which is why they're used to pack more capacitance into a small part. On the exam, the relative dielectric constant for air is 1, not 0, 2 or 4.

params.title: Insulators at UHF
rows: A metal: a conductor, not an insulator

onScreen: Mica: best UHF insulator, very low loss
scenes.narration: At high frequencies, insulators have a weakness. Every time the field reverses, a poor insulator soaks up a little energy and turns it into heat. That's dielectric loss, and at UHF, ultra high frequency, the field reverses so many times each second that the losses pile up. Which material is most useful for insulation at UHF? Mica, because its dielectric loss is very low and it stays stable at high frequencies. Rubber and wax impregnated paper become lossy at those frequencies, wasting energy as heat. And lead doesn't belong on the list at all: it's a metal, a conductor, not an insulator.

blocks.label: Stray current corrosion
blocks.note: Driven from outside, not by the metals

onScreen: 2 dissimilar metals in seawater form a battery
Stray current corrosion: an outside source
scenes.narration: Boats add another enemy: corrosion. Put 2 different metals in seawater, connected together, and you've built a battery. Seawater conducts, so a small current flows from one metal to the other, and the more active metal, the one that gives up its atoms more readily, slowly dissolves. Corrosion resulting from electric current flow between dissimilar metals is called galvanic corrosion. Stray current corrosion is different: it's driven by an outside source, such as current leaking from the boat's wiring, not by the metals themselves. Electrolysis and oxygen starvation corrosion are the other wrong answers. Dissimilar metals, one current between them: galvanic.

params.title: The zinc sacrificial anode
items: Sacrificial anode: a metal fitted to corrode in place of others
Usual choice: a zinc bar
Zinc is more active than bronze, steel and copper
So the zinc corrodes instead of them, and is replaced as it wears

onScreen: Sacrificial anode: corrodes in place of others
More active than bronze, steel and copper
scenes.narration: If the most active metal is the one that corrodes, we can use that on purpose. Bolt a block of a very active metal to the hull and connect it to the other fittings. It becomes the anode, the metal that gives itself up, so it's called a sacrificial anode. The metal usually employed is a zinc bar. Zinc is more active than a vessel's bronze, steel and copper fittings, so the zinc corrodes instead of them. When it's mostly eaten away, you replace it. Platinum, lead and brass are the decoys: none of them is more active than the fittings, so none would corrode in their place.

onScreen: Stainless steel propeller shaft: least affected
scenes.narration: Metals can be lined up from most active to least active in seawater. Zinc sits at the active end, which is why it makes a good anode. An aluminum outdrive, the propeller drive unit that hangs off the back of many powerboats, is also near the active end, so it corrodes readily. Bronze and lead fall in between. At the protected end sits stainless steel. So of common underwater fittings, a stainless steel propeller shaft may be least affected by galvanic corrosion when submerged in seawater. The traps are the bronze through-hull, a fitting that lets water pass through the hull, and the exposed lead keel, the heavy fin under a sailboat.

params.title: The junction diode: a one-way valve
items: Semiconductor, such as silicon: between a conductor and an insulator
N-type: extra free electrons. P-type: a shortage of them
PN junction: where P-type meets N-type; 1 junction makes a diode
Forward: conducts. Reverse: blocks

onScreen: Semiconductor: between a conductor and an insulator
scenes.narration: Our last group of parts is made from semiconductors: materials such as silicon whose conductivity sits between a conductor's and an insulator's. By adding tiny traces of other elements, makers create N-type silicon, N for negative, with extra free electrons, and P-type silicon, P for positive, with a shortage of them. Where P-type meets N-type, you get a PN junction, and a single junction makes a diode. A junction diode works like a one-way valve. Push current the forward way, and charge crosses the junction easily: it conducts. Push the reverse way, and the junction becomes an insulating barrier: it blocks. Diodes turn AC into DC and protect circuits, and their limits are what the exam asks about.

params.title: A junction diode's 2 main ratings
rows: The most current it can carry forward
The most reverse voltage it can block
The junction breaks down and conducts backward

scenes.narration: When you pick a diode, 2 specifications matter most, and they match its 2 jobs. The first is the maximum forward current: how much current it can carry in the forward direction. The second is the PIV, peak inverse voltage: the highest reverse voltage it can block. Inverse just means reverse, and peak means the highest point of the wave, so a diode in an AC circuit must survive the peak, not just the RMS value. Go past the PIV and the junction breaks down and conducts backward. So the 2 most commonly used specifications for a junction diode are maximum forward current and PIV. Reverse current and capacitance are secondary.

params.title: What limits a diode's forward current

onScreen: Exceed it and the diode is destroyed
scenes.narration: So what limits the maximum forward current? Heat. Even while it conducts, a diode has a small voltage across it, called the forward voltage, and that voltage times the current is power, turned into heat right at the junction. More current, more heat. The junction temperature is the limit: let the junction get hotter than its rating, and the diode is destroyed. That's why big diodes are bolted to metal heat sinks, which carry heat away and allow more current. The traps are the PIV, which is a reverse rating, the forward voltage, which only helps make the heat, and back EMF, which belongs to coils.

params.title: The transistor: small signal, big result
items: Amplifier: makes a weak signal stronger
Gain: how many times bigger the output is than the input
Bipolar transistor: base, emitter and collector
A small base current controls a large collector current

onScreen: Amplifier: makes a weak signal stronger
Small base current controls a large current
scenes.narration: Diodes only steer current. A transistor can amplify: make a weak signal, such as the tiny voltage from an antenna, much stronger. How much stronger is called gain. Voltage gain, for example, is the output voltage divided by the input voltage. The most familiar kind is the bipolar transistor, with 3 connections: the base, the emitter and the collector. A small current flowing into the base controls a much larger current flowing from the collector to the emitter. Feed a weak signal into the base, and a bigger copy appears at the collector. Notice that a bipolar transistor's input, the base, has to draw current to work.

params.title: Input impedance: FET versus bipolar
rows: Almost no current at the gate

onScreen: FET: gate draws almost no current, high input impedance
Bipolar: base draws current, low input impedance
scenes.narration: The other big transistor family is the FET, field-effect transistor. Instead of a base current, an FET is controlled by the voltage on its gate, which sets up an electric field that opens or pinches off a channel for current. The gate draws almost no current. That brings us to input impedance: how much an input opposes current from whatever drives it. An input that draws almost no current has high input impedance; an input that draws current has low input impedance. So an FET has high input impedance, and a bipolar transistor has low input impedance, because its base draws current. The supply voltage doesn't change that answer.

onScreen: JFET, MOSFET and GaAsFET: separate FET families
scenes.narration: FETs come in separate families. The JFET, junction field-effect transistor, uses a PN junction at its gate. The MOSFET, metal oxide semiconductor field-effect transistor, insulates its gate with a thin layer of oxide. The GaAsFET, gallium arsenide FET, is used at very high frequencies. JFETs are sorted by the material that forms their channel, the path current takes through the transistor. So the 2 basic types of junction field-effect transistor are N-channel and P-channel. MOSFET and GaAsFET is a trap answer: those are separate FET families, not JFET types. High and low power, or silicon and germanium, aren't the basic types either.

blocks.label: Static or excessive voltage
blocks.note: Could punch through the gate oxide

onScreen: Static or excessive voltage threatens the thin gate oxide
Built-in Zener diode clamps the voltage
scenes.narration: That thin oxide layer in a MOSFET's gate is its weak spot. It's far thinner than a hair, so a static charge from your fingers or an excessive voltage can punch right through it and ruin the transistor. To protect it, MOSFETs are manufactured with a Zener diode built into the gate. A Zener diode is a diode designed to break down and conduct in reverse at a set voltage. Normally it does nothing, but when a dangerous voltage arrives, it conducts, clamping the voltage, or holding it down, before the oxide is damaged. The exam's decoys are the Schottky diode, the tunnel diode and the metal oxide varistor.

params.title: Common emitter versus common collector
rows: Collector; output follows at the emitter

onScreen: Common collector: voltage gain slightly below 1
scenes.narration: For the last exam fact, back to the bipolar transistor. Its amplifier circuits are named for the connection that the input and the output share, called the common terminal. In a common emitter amplifier, the signal goes in at the base and comes out at the collector, and it provides both voltage gain and current gain. In a common collector amplifier, also called an emitter follower, the output at the emitter simply follows the input, so its voltage gain is slightly below 1. It's still useful as a go-between that feeds a load drawing lots of current, but it doesn't boost voltage. So a common emitter amplifier has more voltage gain than a common collector. The trap says less.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Watt = 1 joule per second = 1 volt × 1 ampere; silver and copper conduct best
Current makes magnetism; a changing field induces a voltage that opposes it
Meters read RMS: outlet 117 V, peak 165.5 V; × 1.414 for peak, × 0.9 for average
Capacitor: electric field, blocks DC. Coil: magnetic field, X<sub>L</sub> = 2π f L
Apparent power × power factor = true power; reactive power does no net work

onScreen: True power = apparent power × power factor
scenes.narration: To wrap up, here's what to carry into the rest of Element 3. Voltage pushes, current flows, and resistance holds it back. Power is volts times amps, in watts: 1 joule per second. Silver and copper conduct best. Current makes a magnetic field, and a changing field induces a voltage that opposes the change. AC meters read RMS: the outlet's 117 volts, times 1.414 for the peak of 165.5 volts, and times 0.9 for the average. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field and blocks DC; a coil stores it in a magnetic field, with a reactance of two pi f L. And apparent power times the power factor gives true power, while reactive power does no net work. Well done.
